stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement set by the Reconstruction Act of 1867 for southern states’ readmission to the Union?
options: Black people had to be allowed to participate in state conventions and state elections.
The state had to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution.
The state had to pay reparations and provide land grants to all former enslaved people.
The state had to rewrite its constitution and ratify it.
explanation: The Reconstruction Act of 1867, Congress’s plan for the rehabilitation of the South, was much harsher than President Johnson’s plan. Johnson, like Lincoln (who began planning the method for readmitting southern states before his assassination), wanted a reconciliatory plan that punished only the most prominent leaders of the secession. Radical Republicans in Congress wanted something much tougher, and Johnson’s plan was so lenient (in the first postwar Congress, Johnson’s plan would have allowed the former president of the Confederacy to take a seat in the Senate) that it drove many moderates into the radicals’ camp. The result was the Reconstruction Act, a punitive measure that imposed a number of strict requirements on southern states as preconditions for their readmission to the Union. Choices (A), (B), and (D) list all of those preconditions; the fact that Congress did not impose any requirements such as the one described in (C) pretty much doomed postwar southern Black people to poverty.

stem: Which battle gave Lincoln the victory he needed to issue the Emancipation Proclamation?
options: Gettysburg
Antietam
Fort Sumter
Harper’s Ferry
explanation: In September of 1862, the Battle of Antietam gave President Lincoln the victory he needed to issue the Emancipation Proclamation from a position of apparent strength. Because the confederates had been advancing north up until that time, Lincoln feared that issuing the Proclamation without a clear victory would seem like a desperate act. The Emancipation Proclamation was issued four months later in January of 1863.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding social issues in the post-Civil War 19th century is true?
options: African Americans struggled against discriminatory practices even though the case of Plessy v. Ferguson technically outlawed legal segregation.
While African Americans and women achieved suffrage during this period, both groups were often kept from voting through various illegal means.
Impoverished southerners, both Black and white, had greater opportunities for upward mobility than did their northern counterparts due to sharecropping and the crop lien system.
The influx of immigrant factory workers and the development of mass transportation caused the middle class to largely flee the major cities.
explanation: In the post-war 19th century the Industrial Revolution caused an influx in many major cities of poor immigrants seeking low-paying factory jobs. Parts of these cities became overcrowded, economically depressed, and crime-ridden, and many middle-class Americans, aided by modern transportation systems, consequently fled the areas—keep (D). African Americans struggled against discrimination and segregation, and the case of Plessy v. Ferguson facilitated such unfair treatment, holding that “separate but equal” accommodations were constitutional, so (A) is incorrect. While Black men were granted the right to vote in 1870, no woman of any race could vote until the Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920, granting suffrage to all women. Choice (B) is incorrect. Sharecropping, based on the crop lien system, served to keep poor farmers, both Black and white, in constant debt and offered little opportunity to improve one’s lot, so (C) is incorrect.

stem: Which of the following statements about Supreme Court decisions during the latter part of the 19th century is most accurate?
options: They reduced federal power over the states by narrowly defining the applicability of the Constitution to state law.
They cleared the way for the liberal reforms of the 20th century by broadly interpreting constitutional guarantees of individual rights.
They had little practical effect because the executive branch consistently refused to enforce the Court’s rulings.
They used the Fourteenth Amendment to create numerous environmental regulations and human rights, stifling American business growth.
explanation: If you remember that the Supreme Court of the late 19th century was extremely conservative and extremely pro-business—and you should remember that, because it’s important—you should have been able to eliminate (B) and (D) immediately. If you remember the profound impact of such decisions as Plessy v. Ferguson —and you should also remember that—you could have eliminated (C).

stem: The term vertical integration refers to
options: Reconstruction-Era efforts to assimilate newly freed enslaved people into all social strata of American society
an architectural movement that sought to blend urban skyscrapers with the natural landscape surrounding them
the industrial practice of assigning workers a single, repetitive task in order to maximize productivity
control of all aspects of an industry, from production of raw materials to delivery of finished goods
explanation: “Vertical integration” is another name for monopoly. Monopolies ran rampant in the late 1800s; the government did little to prevent them, and the courts actively encouraged them. Of the incorrect answers, (C) refers to assembly line production, and (A) and (B) are just made up.

stem: The passage of the Pendleton Act was a direct result of the
options: assassination of Abraham Lincoln
failure of Reconstruction
assassination of James A. Garfield
Supreme Court decision in Plessy v. Ferguson
explanation: James A. Garfield’s presidency is remembered for one thing: Garfield’s assassination at the hands of a disgruntled office seeker. His assassin, Charles Guiteau, was actually a mentally disturbed individual who imagined himself an important player in Garfield’s electoral success. Guiteau convinced himself that he deserved a big fat government job as a reward for his efforts, and when he received none he retaliated by shooting Garfield. Garfield’s successor, Chester Arthur, signed the Pendleton Act, which replaced the spoils system Guiteau had hoped to exploit with a merit-based system for selecting civil servants.

stem: The Haymarket Riot represented a major setback for the
options: women’s suffrage movement
civil rights movement for African Americans
Knights of Labor
temperance movement
explanation: Although one might certainly make a valid claim that labor unions were necessary during the late 19th century when working conditions were dangerous, unsanitary, and exploitative, unions were very unpopular because they were associated with political radicalism and violence. The 1886 Haymarket Riot began at a mass meeting organized by anarchists in Haymarket Square, Chicago, to protest events related to a strike at the nearby McCormick Harvester Company plant. When police tried to break up the meeting, someone threw a bomb into the crowd, leaving seven police officers dead and several wounded. This incident convinced the American public that unions were dangerous and ultimately led to the decline of the Knights of Labor.

stem: Japan was outraged by the American annexation of Hawaii in 1898 primarily because
options: Japan depended heavily on trade with Hawaii to support its economy
the United States had signed a treaty with Japan granting Japan rights to Hawaii
the Japanese were committed to the principle of self-rule throughout the Pacific
nearly half of Hawaii’s residents were of Japanese descent
explanation: If you can’t immediately identify the correct answer to this one, use common sense to eliminate incorrect answers. Japan is a huge nation relative to Hawaii; its economy couldn’t realistically depend on trade with the island, so eliminate (A). Choice (B) contradicts one of the main themes of the period—the Age of Imperialism, when every Western power, including the United States, was gathering colonies in the East. Would the United States have ceded Hawaii to Japan during that period? Unlikely, and much less likely still that the AP Exam would ask about an anomalous agreement. Choice (C) suggests Japan was a bastion of democracy in the late 19th century; in fact, it was ruled by an emperor.

stem: The “new immigrants” who arrived in the United States after the Civil War were different from the “old immigrants” in that they
options: came mostly from Latin American countries
settled in rural areas in the Midwest where land was plentiful
were better prepared than previous immigrants had been to face the challenges of urban life
came from southern and eastern Europe, speaking unfamiliar languages
explanation: Historians describe the immigrants who came to the United States before the Civil War as “old immigrants.” These groups came predominantly from countries in northwestern Europe. For the most part, they were Protestants and spoke English and easily became part of the melting pot we call America. Following the Civil War, however, the “new immigrants” came predominantly from nations in South and Eastern Europe, including Russians, Italians, and Poles. Many of these people were Catholics and Jews and were culturally very different from most Americans by that point. These new immigrants were not easily assimilated. They tended to settle among themselves in ethnic neighborhoods in major cities like New York and Chicago where there was a demand for unskilled labor in the numerous factories of these big cities.

stem: The “Ghost Dance” movement among Western Native Americans stressed all of the following EXCEPT
options: the belief that the world would soon come to an end
the rejection of alcohol and other trappings of white society
unity among Native Americans of different tribes
nonviolence
explanation: The Ghost Dancers arose in the late 1800s when the sad fate awaiting the great Native American tribes of the era was becoming all too apparent. Wovoka, of the Paiute people, started the Ghost Dance movement, which resembled a religious revival. It centered on a dance ritual that enabled participants to envision a brighter future, one in which white people no longer dominated North America. Wovoka preached unity among Native Americans and the rejection of white culture and its trappings, especially alcohol. He also preached the imminent end of the world, at which point the Native American dead would rise to reclaim the land that was rightfully theirs. Sioux Ghost Dancers believed in the power of “ghost shirts,” garments blessed by spiritual leaders that were capable of stopping bullets. This belief led to a rise in Sioux militancy and ultimately contributed to their massacre at Wounded Knee in 1890.

stem: In the late 19th century, political machines such as Tammany Hall were successful primarily because
options: they operated primarily in rural areas, where the government could not monitor their activities
they focused on accomplishing only a narrow set of human rights objectives
they championed the suffragettes and received their support in return
machine politicians provided needed jobs and services to naturalized citizens in return for their votes
explanation: Waves of European immigration throughout the 19th century swelled cities’ populations. Governments of the time were nowhere near as activist as they are today, and only a very few provided even minimal services to immigrants as they accommodated themselves to their new homeland; ethnic communities and churches were expected to provide such services. A number of enterprising, unscrupulous men recognized the opportunity to develop great political power with these immigrants. Such men, known as political bosses, helped immigrants find homes and jobs and acquire citizenship and voting rights. In essence, these bosses created entire communities and then provided them with all sorts of services: food and loans for the poor, parks and protection for the community. In return, the communities were expected to provide loyal political support, which they did, originally out of loyalty, and later, as the machines became extremely powerful, out of both loyalty and fear. The bosses could then hand an election to a politician of their choice, in return for favors. Political machines filled a need, albeit in an expensive and unethical way. stem: All of the following states were admitted to the union in the post-war 19th century EXCEPT
options: North Dakota
Wyoming
Arizona
Washington
explanation: Arizona was not admitted to the union until 1912.

stem: Which of the following was NOT associated with the westward expansion of railroads during the mid- to late 19th century?
options: The social doctrine of Manifest Destiny
Increased confrontation between settlers and Western Native American tribes
The economic decline and loss of political influence of Tammany Hall
The emergence of the Populist movement
explanation: The westward expansion of the United States (driven by newly acquired lands from the Mexican Cession and the Gadsden Purchase) during the mid- to late 19th century was quickly aided by the expansion of railroads and the desire and perceived right of Americans to explore and settle the West consistent with the doctrine of Manifest Destiny. One result of this expansion was increased confrontation between settlers and tribes. Ultimately, the power and influence of railroad magnates such as Vanderbilt led to the emergence of political movements to regulate the railroads, such as the Grange movement and the later Populist movement. Tammany Hall was based in New York and had little to do with westward expansion.

stem: Muckrakers furthered the causes of the Progressive movement by
options: organizing grassroots campaigns for political reform at the state level
suing large companies and donating their court awards to Progressive campaigns
staging large, violent protests in support of Progressive goals
alerting the public to the social ills and corporate corruption targeted by Progressives
explanation: “Muckrakers” is a term Theodore Roosevelt coined to describe the investigative journalists of his day. They included Ida Tarbell, whose book on Standard Oil revealed corruption in the oil industry and big business in general; Upton Sinclair, whose stomach-turning account of the meatpacking industry drove public outcry for government regulation of food production (the Food and Drug Administration was created as a result of Sinclair’s book The Jungle ); and Lincoln Steffens, whose The Shame of the Cities exposed many Americans to the extent of urban poverty and corruption in urban government. Muckrakers helped fuel the public outcry for government reform, the main goal of the Progressive movement.

stem: Keynesian economic theory would assert that
options: government interference in economics for the purpose of remedying a depression will only make matters worse
the way to avoid an economic depression is for people to start saving a high percentage of their incomes as soon as the economy takes a downturn
economic depressions worsen when individuals buy what they cannot comfortably afford
lavish spending during an economic depression should be encouraged
explanation: Economist John Maynard Keynes theorized that a depression is the result of a vicious cycle: an economic downturn causes people to become anxious and reluctant to spend money, which leads businesses to fail and the economy to worsen, which leads to even greater anxiety and reluctance to spend money, which exacerbates the economic situation, etc. The way to stop the cycle and improve the economy is, perhaps counterintuitively, for people to spend money freely during times of hardship. The government can facilitate this process by providing its citizens with funds, whether through jobs or handouts, which they will presumably spend and thereby stimulate the economy. Roosevelt’s policies during the Great Depression were based on Keynesian economics.

stem: Following the Spanish–American War and the acquisition of territory overseas, in a series of cases known as the Insular Cases, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that
options: natives living on American soil abroad were guaranteed the same rights and privileges as U.S. citizens living within the continental United States
colonial subjects within the American Empire were not entitled to the rights guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution
“the Constitution follows the flag”
Congress must relinquish control of these overseas possessions and honor their right of self-determination
explanation: As a result of winning the Spanish–American War in 1898, the United States acquired Guam, Puerto Rico, the Philippines, and for all intents and purposes, Cuba. (Although we had claimed we had no interest in acquiring Cuba and could empathize with its colonial status, having once been a colony ourselves, the Platt Amendment rendered the island a virtual colony of the United States.) The situation in the Philippines created intense debate between business interests that saw the enormous economic benefits to acquiring “stepping stones” to profitable Chinese trade, and those Americans who believed having colonies contradicted our fundamental democratic principles. Once we acquired overseas possessions, a question arose as to the rights and privileges of the Native peoples living within the American Empire. In a series of Supreme Court cases known as the Insular Cases, the Court ruled that the “Constitution did not follow the flag,” and thus, colonial subjects were not entitled to the same rights as U.S. citizens living at home or abroad.

stem: Which of the following best summarizes the contents of the Zimmermann telegram, which was intercepted in 1917?
options: Germany offered Mexico an alliance and help regaining land lost in the Mexican Cession if Mexico attacked the United States
A British spy alerted the world to the existence of mass extermination camps in German-held territories.
The United States assured the British that it would join the war in Europe if the war were to continue for another year.
The owner of the Boston Red Sox revealed a plan to sell star player Babe Ruth to the New York Yankees for a large amount of cash.
explanation: This is a straight recall question. You either know what the Zimmermann telegram is or you don’t. If you know it, you’re going to get this question right. If you don’t, use Process of Elimination to get rid of anachronistic answers, as in (B), or answers that seem un-AP-like because they don’t reinforce important themes of U.S. history, as in (D). You should know, however, that the Zimmermann telegram was one of the reasons the United States entered World War I.

stem: During World War I, the propaganda effort headed by the Committee on Public Information used all of the following techniques to build public support for the war EXCEPT
options: influencing schoolteachers to include lessons on patriotism
mandating a sugar ration of one pound per week
producing prowar posters, buttons, short films, and other media
training people to speak publicly at movie theaters, churches, lodges, and other organizations
explanation: The Committee on Public Information was only in existence for three years, but it managed to build, from nothing, a vast propaganda movement that reoriented the American public toward war. This was no small task, seeing as how the United States had maintained a policy and culture of isolationism for the previous century. Choices (A), (C), and (D) were all duties of the CPI, so eliminate them. Rationing of sugar during World War I was a historical fact, but it wasn’t the responsibility of the CPI; therefore, (B) is correct.

stem: Wilson’s Fourteen Points plan for peace after World War I included all of the following EXCEPT
options: promotion of universal self-determination
lower tariffs to promote free trade
repayment of all Allied war expenses by Germany
across-the-board arms reductions
explanation: In the aftermath of World War I, President Wilson favored a peace that would promote openness in international affairs, free trade, and diplomacy. He also sought universal arms reductions and a mechanism for enforcing world peace, which was to be achieved through the League of Nations. He did not seek a punitive treaty that forced Germany to pay heavy reparations; the European allies, however, insisted. Wilson was able to negotiate very little of his Fourteen Points plan, but he remained optimistic that the League of Nations would eventually broker a fairer postwar peace. Unfortunately, Wilson’s hopes were never realized.

stem: All of the following can be seen as clashes between traditional and modern culture during the Post–World War I Era EXCEPT
options: the rise of the Ku Klux Klan
the Teapot Dome Scandal
the Scopes Monkey Trial
the Emergency Quota Act
explanation: The Ku Klux Klan evoked the execrable southern traditions of racism and physical intimidation against the modern drive for expanded civil rights. The Scopes Monkey Trial pitted religion against the modern notion of evolution. The Emergency Quota Act was passed to check immigration from non-western European countries; its champions felt the nation’s Western European traditions were threatened by immigrants from Southern Europe, Eastern Europe, South America, and Asia. The Teapot Dome Scandal, on the other hand, was just an example of good old-fashioned political corruption.

stem: The stock market crash of 1929 was the result of which of the following? Irresponsible lending by banks and corporations Overspeculation of the value of the stock market Failure of banks to guarantee the security of deposits
options: II only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II, and III
explanation: While there were many factors that contributed the stock market crash in October 1929, the leading contributors were apparent overspeculation of the value of the market, which was driven up by lending and irresponsible investing based on the “guarantee” of future profits, a principle known as buying on margin. Much of the lending and support for these transactions was contributed by banks who saw some of the greatest losses and were shuttered during the collapse, leading many Americans to lose their balances in the bank overnight. The FDIC, formed early during Roosevelt’s administration, guaranteed bank deposits backed by the strength of the U.S. government.

stem: Which of the following was NOT a New Deal policy?
options: Federal insurance for banks in order to ensure the confidence of depositors
Stricter laws against unionizing in order to prevent loss of income due to strikes
Payments to farmers who agreed to substantially reduce production in order to stabilize prices
Government regulation of the stock market in order to protect investors
explanation: Roosevelt adopted a pro-union stance regarding the New Deal, believing that the right to collective bargaining was critical to ensuring decent wages for workers. Americans would have more money to spend if they were adequately paid, and increased spending would benefit the economy.

stem: The Nye Commission report of 1936 reinforced American isolationism by
options: revealing unethical profiteering by American munitions companies during World War I
concluding that Germany had no interest in engaging the United States in war
listing the domestic programs that would have to be forfeited if the United States were to increase its overseas commitments
detailing deficiencies in all branches of the U.S. military
explanation: Americans were already predisposed to isolationism before they heard the results of the Nye Commission’s investigations. They had been promised that World War I was “the war to end all wars.” Less than 20 years later, Europe was on the verge of another big confrontation. The sentiment in the United States was, “Let them sort this out themselves.” Those feelings were strengthened when the Nye Commission revealed that many American munitions companies had violated an arms embargo in order to arm the nation’s enemies. It further revealed that U.S. banks had lobbied for entry into the war in order to protect more than $2 billion in loans to Britain and its allies. The report left Americans more cynical about the motives of its leaders and less susceptible to calls for intervention overseas.

stem: In its Korematsu v. United States (1944) decision, the Supreme Court ruled that
options: the wartime relocation of West Coast Japanese Americans was not unconstitutional
the Japanese government had no legitimate claim to reparations for the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
the U.S. government had violated the Constitution by entering the Korean War
immigration quotas based on race were unconstitutional
explanation: Fred Korematsu was among the more than 110,000 Japanese Americans ordered to relocate from the West Coast to internment camps during World War II. Korematsu refused, was arrested, and took his case all the way to the Supreme Court. The Court ruled that the government had not exceeded its power, noting that extraordinary times sometimes call for extraordinary measures; three of the nine justices dissented. History has not judged Roosevelt’s internment policy kindly. In 1998, Fred Korematsu was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

stem: All of the following threatened Harry Truman’s chances for re-election in 1948 EXCEPT
options: Truman’s positions on civil rights
rampant inflation
the Dixiecrat candidacy of Strom Thurmond
public dissatisfaction with the Korean War
explanation: The Korean War didn’t begin until 1950.

stem: Loyalty oaths, blacklists, and Alger Hiss are all associated with the
options: civil rights movement
New Deal
Red Scare
Great Society
explanation: Fear of communist infiltration and subversion reached hysterical proportions in the Post–World War II Era, making all sorts of excessive responses to the communist threat not only possible but likely. Loyalty oaths were instituted by private companies, state governments, and even the federal government, based on the apparent belief that communist spies are capable of espionage but not of lying under oath. Blacklists banned suspected subversives from work in many industries, destroying the lives of many innocent people. Alger Hiss was accused of passing government secrets to the Soviet Union. He professed his innocence to his dying day, although Soviet files released in the Post-Soviet Era suggest his guilt. The Hiss case was front-page news. Richard Nixon played a prominent role in Hiss’s prosecution, thereby earning Nixon the national spotlight for the first time.

stem: John Foster Dulles, secretary of state under Eisenhower, intensified Cold War rhetoric with Washington’s New Look defense program that emphasized
options: threatening Moscow with “massive retaliation”
expanding conventional forces in Europe
pursuing summit diplomacy with the Soviets
conducting shuttle diplomacy in the Middle East
explanation: The key to this question is the phrase “intensified Cold War rhetoric.” Words like “massive retaliation” didn’t exactly improve relations with the Soviet Union. While (B), containment, was the guiding principle of U.S. foreign policy throughout the Cold War, this question is asking something more specific. And although Dulles did forge many alliances with smaller nations (collective security), (A) is a better answer. Choice (C), summit diplomacy, was practiced by Reagan and Gorbachev, while the term “shuttle diplomacy,” (D), was applied to Henry Kissinger under Nixon.

stem: The Cold War policy of containment and concern with national defense played a background role in the development of all of the following programs or projects EXCEPT
options: the Interstate Highway Act
the Peace Corps
the Berlin Wall
the Central Intelligence Agency
explanation: The influence of the policy of containment could be seen across many U.S. policies and programs, though in some not-so-obvious ways. For example, the Interstate Highway Act was intended to build a national highway system both for civilian use and to facilitate national defense, if needed: eliminate (A). The Peace Corps was created to send exemplary young Americans around the world to not only persuade young people in other countries that war wasn’t necessary—but also that the American system of capitalism created happier, healthier, more helpful citizens than communism did. This was a “soft” form of containment; eliminate (B). Likewise, while the government had established other intelligence organizations previously, the Central Intelligence Agency was founded in 1947 to not only centralize all intelligence but also to aim more specifically at gathering information about the Soviet Union. Eliminate (D). The Berlin Wall was certainly a literal type of containment, but it was built by the Soviet Union across the city of Berlin, Germany, and its construction was unrelated to the U.S. government. Choice (C) is correct.

stem: Which of the following is true regarding leftist political groups in the 1960s?
options: Their leadership tended to be female dominated in keeping with feminist ideals.
They were sharply divided in terms of those who supported the Vietnam War and those who opposed it.
They were fiercely opposed to the Warren Court on ideological grounds.
They caused a conservative backlash in the 1970s.
explanation: The radical leftist politics of the 1960s caused a conservative reaction in the 1970s, with the formation of many groups that advocated for a return to traditional American values on issues such as abortion, affirmative action, sexual morality, etc. However, leftist political groups in the 1960s were unified in their opposition to the Vietnam War and were ideologically aligned with the highly liberal Supreme Court under Earl Warren (although some believed the Court did not push the liberal agenda hard enough). While some groups took a strong feminist stance, most remained male-dominated, with women serving in supporting roles.

stem: The Korean War
options: ended with the surrender of communist forces to the Americans in 1953
resulted in substantial territorial gains for South Korea with respect to its prewar northern boundary
demonstrated that the United States was reluctant to engage China in full-blown military conflict
exemplified the willingness of the executive branch to defer to the military judgment of generals during wartime
explanation: President Truman, understanding the magnitude and potential consequences of going to war with communist China, refused to allow General Douglas MacArthur to launch a full-blown attack on Chinese forces when China entered the war in support of North Korea. When MacArthur publicly criticized the president for this decision, Truman fired MacArthur for insubordination—so (D) is incorrect. American troops did not advance, the parties signed an armistice in 1953, and the North–South Korean border remained at approximately the 38th parallel (the prewar boundary).

stem: Which of the following does NOT accurately describe the presidential election of 1968?
options: The Democratic Party was fractured because of dissent over the Vietnam War.
A frontrunner for one of the major parties was assassinated during the primary season.
Both major-party candidates campaigned as Washington outsiders.
A third-party candidacy split the traditionally Democratic southern vote.
explanation: The Republican candidate, Richard Nixon, was a former vice president. The Democratic candidate, Hubert Humphrey, was the current vice president and, before that, a longtime senator. Neither could have campaigned as a Washington outsider, and neither did. The Democrats were fractured over the war; the party was home to both aggressive cold warriors and the antiwar movement. Robert Kennedy was assassinated in June; many believe he would have won the nomination had he not been killed. George Wallace formed a third party and campaigned on states’ rights and segregation, siphoning off key votes in the South, where the Democrats had traditionally done well. Nixon’s only opposition in the Republican primaries came from Nelson D. Rockefeller, who campaigned halfheartedly, and Ronald Reagan, who, at the time, was seen as too extreme to ever win the presidency. Reagan never changed, but the country did.

stem: Inflation throughout the 1970s was driven in large part by
options: the cost of funding the Vietnam War
rapidly increasing gasoline and oil prices
government investment in the space program
a dramatic reduction of income tax rates
explanation: Gasoline and oil prices shot through the roof in the 1970s, affecting a wide range of industries that relied on the fuels to run. The result was widespread inflation throughout the decade.

stem: The incident that began a chain of events that became one of the most infamous presidential scandals in American history and eventually led to the resignation of Richard Nixon was the
options: burglary of Daniel Ellsberg’s psychiatrist’s office
political sabotage of Nixon’s opponent, George McGovern
illegal use of the CIA to hush up the FBI’s investigation of the events surrounding the publication of the Pentagon Papers
break-in and attempted bugging of the Democratic Party’s national headquarters
explanation: This is the event that started it all—the break-in to the Watergate complex in Washington, D.C., where the Democratic Party had its national headquarters. All of the other choices became part of the cover-up and are known collectively as “Watergate,” which ultimately forced the resignation of Richard Nixon, the only president to resign in American history. Nixon resigned before he was impeached and was subsequently pardoned by Gerald Ford.

stem: What was the final result of the Vietnam War?
options: The United States won a victory in the armed conflict and secured a democratic ally in the region.
The United States withdrew and the nation became a single nation united under communist rule.
The Vietnam War ended in a stalemate resulting in geographic division of the nation of Vietnam into democratic and communist nations.
The Vietnam War has never ceased and armed conflicts between democratic and communist factions within the nation continue today.
explanation: Under increasing social and political pressure, the United States withdrew from Vietnam and ultimately the communist-backed forces of North Vietnam secured victory and united the nation as a communist state in 1975.

stem: A major paradox of Richard Nixon’s administration was that
options: the globalists who voted for him were disappointed by his isolationist foreign policy
the foreign powers who wanted him to end the Vietnam War were shocked when he actually extended it
his condemnation of corruption while on the campaign trail in 1968 was contradicted by his own downfall in the Watergate scandal in 1974
Nixon, a conservative Republican, enacted progressive legislation on domestic issues including workplace safety and the environment
explanation: While Nixon’s foreign policy was the “best of times, worst of times”—he and Secretary of State Kissinger opened China but carpetbombed Cambodia—some of his domestic policy was surprisingly liberal. He created OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health Administration), signed the Clean Air and Clean Water acts, and established the Environmental Protection Agency. Choice (A) is a reversal: the isolationists who voted for him were disappointed by his re-engagement with China, so eliminate (A). Nixon ended the Vietnam War, which is quite the opposite of extending it, so eliminate (B). Nixon didn’t run on the idea of condemnation of corruption in 1968, so eliminate (C).

stem: Each of the following is associated with the Reagan presidency EXCEPT
options: trickle-down economics
New Federalism
the Whitewater scandal
Star Wars
explanation: The Whitewater scandal occurred during the 1990s and involved questionable real-estate dealings by President Clinton. “Trickle-down” theory was Reagan’s economic policy involving corporate tax cuts and New Federalism was his plan to shift federal power to the states. “Star Wars” refers to the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), a space-based missile shield program proposed by Reagan as a means of protecting the United States against a nuclear attack by the Soviet Union.

stem: Since the end of the Cold War, the continuing American impulse to intervene in the economic and political affairs of other nations around the world is motivated by all of the following EXCEPT
options: fears of renewed Soviet expansion
the protection of human rights
American economic interests
the desire to promote and develop democratic institutions in former communist and Third World nations
explanation: Though American relations with Russia remain uneasy, fears of Soviet expansion are a thing of the past; the Soviet Union ceased to exist in 1991, ending the Cold War.

stem: All of the following acts of President Ronald Reagan’s administration are characterized as a return to conservative political values EXCEPT
options: cuts in the federal budget
nominating Sandra Day O'Connor to the Court
tax cuts for corporations
the loosening of government regulation
explanation: In 1981, Ronald Reagan, in a move supported by various groups across the political spectrum, made Sandra Day O’Connor the first woman to serve on the Supreme Court. All the other choices represent typically conservative policy decisions by Reagan.

stem: Which of the following did NOT contribute to the emergence of the New Right of the 1970s and 1980s?
options: The Moral Majority movement
The popularity of Ronald Reagan
The “stagflation” economic condition of the 1970s
A sudden drop in the stock market
explanation: Although there was a brief drop in the stock market in 1987 (known as Black Monday), this was not a contributing factor to the emergence of the New Right. All of the other factors did lead to this renewal of conservatism.

stem: Which of the following happened during the 2000 presidential election?
options: George W. Bush won the popular vote.
Al Gore won the popular vote.
The Supreme Court ordered a recount in Florida, after which Bush was declared the winner.

stem: The above excerpts support which one of the following generalizations?
stimulus: Source 1: “He who is by nature not his own but another’s man, is by nature a slave; and he may be said to be another’s man who, being a human being, is also a possession.” Source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I (c. 350 BCE; Benjamin Jowett translation, 1885 — public domain). Source 2: Paraphrased from Mary Ann Glendon, “The Forgotten Crucible: The Latin American Influence on the Universal Human Rights Idea” (2003). Glendon argues that as Latin American nations gained independence in the nineteenth century, two intellectual strains merged with an older, more universalist natural-law tradition to produce a distinctively Latin American discourse of rights. She traces its roots to the Spanish Dominicans — above all Bartolomé de Las Casas, the sixteenth-century bishop who condemned slavery and defended Native peoples on the basis of a natural right to liberty grounded in a single common humanity: “All the peoples of the world are humans,” Las Casas wrote, “and all the races of humankind are one.” Following Paolo Carozza and Brian Tierney, Glendon credits Las Casas and his fellow Dominicans with laying the groundwork for a doctrine of natural rights independent of religious revelation, drawn instead from human rationality and free will and from Aristotelian philosophy.
options: After European and Latin American populations interacted economically, most Europeans were more compassionate toward the interests of non-white people.

The appeal to natural rights and natural law succeeded in abolishing slavery in the New World.
The European belief in white superiority was used to justify the doctrine of natural rights.
explanation: Correct: (B). Source 1 states Aristotle’s “natural slave” doctrine — that some people are by nature suited to be ruled — which Spanish thinkers drew on to justify the subjugation of Native peoples. Source 2 traces the opposing tradition: Las Casas and the Spanish Dominicans argued for a natural right to liberty grounded in a common humanity, a tradition Glendon credits with shaping later human-rights thought. The two excerpts therefore document a genuine debate over how Native peoples should be treated, which is exactly what (B) says — rule out (A). Neither source says anything about abolishing slavery, so rule out (C). And the natural-rights doctrine in the second excerpt was used to challenge, not justify, claims of white superiority, so rule out (D).

stem: The author would be most supportive of which of the following claims?

explanation: The United States almost fought a war over the Oregon Territory, which consisted of present-day Oregon, Washington, and parts of Montana and Idaho.
